name: Shenstone
text: Your train passes near Shenstone, on the train's {side}, once the manufacturing home of Norton motorcycles. Henry Sanders, the village's curate from 1755 to 1770, wrote The History and Antiquities of Shenstone, described as a model parish history.

name: Sutton Coldfield transmitting station
text: Your train passes near the Sutton Coldfield transmitting station, on the train's {side}, which on December 17th 1949 became the first television transmitter to broadcast outside London and the Home Counties. By population covered it is the third most important transmitter in the UK, and its mast is 270.5 metres tall.

name: Four Oaks
text: Your train passes near Four Oaks, on the train's {side}, where Henry Folliott built Four Oaks Hall in 1677; a later owner added a deer park. The estate was sold for housing in 1868, about 200 large houses went up between 1895 and 1915, and the neglected hall was pulled down in 1898.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Sutton Coldfield
text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church, on the train's {side}, the Grade I listed parish church of Sutton Coldfield. Its west tower dates from the late 15th century; Bishop John Vesey added the side aisles in the 1530s, and his tomb is inside; and its early 17th-century screens and panelling came from Worcester Cathedral.

name: Sutton Coldfield Town Hall
text: Your train passes near the Town Hall, on the train's {side}, opened in 1906 next to Sutton Coldfield's Council House, which began as the Royal Hotel, built in 1865 on a hill above the newly opened station. Now a theatre and events venue, it has a clock tower that also served as a hose tower for the fire brigade.

name: Highbury Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Highbury Theatre, on the train's {side}, one of the oldest amateur theatres in Birmingham. Its company began as a play-reading circle in 1924 and built the theatre largely with their own hands from a First World War mission chapel, bought in 1937; some of its seats, from a bombed city theatre, bore bomb splinters.

name: Erdington Abbey
text: Your train passes near Erdington Abbey, on the train's {side}, the Roman Catholic church of Saints Thomas and Edmund, opened in 1850 to Charles Hansom's design: its steeple is 117 feet high, the same as the building's length. In 1876 it was handed to Benedictine monks from Beuron in Germany, exiled during Bismarck's Kulturkampf.

name: Mothers
text: Your train passes near the site of Mothers, on the train's {side}, a club above a furniture store in Erdington High Street from 1968 to 1971, where more than 400 acts played. Pink Floyd recorded part of Ummagumma live there in April 1969, and Billboard magazine voted it the number one rock venue in the world.

name: National Memorial Arboretum
text: Your train passes near the National Memorial Arboretum, on the train's {side}, opened in 2001 on about 150 acres of old gravel workings. Its more than 25,000 trees stand among more than 400 memorials, including the Armed Forces Memorial, where at 11am on November 11th the sun shines through slits in its walls onto a wreath.

name: Croxall Lakes
text: Your train passes Croxall Lakes, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve made from sand and gravel pits that were quarried in the 1990s and left to flood. It lies where the Tame and the Mease meet the Trent, which makes it an important stopping point for migrating birds.

name: Alvecote Priory
text: Your train passes the remains of Alvecote Priory, on the train's {side}, a small Benedictine priory founded in 1159 as a dependency of Great Malvern Priory. Little is left, but its main entrance arch still stands about 20 feet high, and its dovecote survives.

name: Polesworth Abbey
text: Your train passes near the site of Polesworth Abbey, on the train's {side}, a Benedictine nunnery whose 12th-century church is now the parish church of St Editha, with its 14th-century gatehouse still standing. After the Dissolution, the Goodere family built Polesworth Hall on the site, and Sir Henry Goodere led the Polesworth Group of poets, among them his protégé Michael Drayton.

name: St Peter's Church, Mancetter
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church in Mancetter, on the train's {side}, whose chancel walls still include 12th-century masonry. In Roman times a legionary fortress was built here by about AD 50, where Watling Street crosses the River Anker, and Mancetter has been suggested as a possible site of Boudica's defeat, though the exact place is unknown.

name: St Nicolas Church, Nuneaton
text: Your train passes near St Nicolas Church, on the train's {side}, Nuneaton's Grade I listed parish church, dating from around 1340. George Eliot used it as Milby Church in Scenes of Clerical Life; all but one of its stained glass windows were destroyed by bombing in 1941.

name: Griff House
text: Your train passes near Griff House, on the train's {side}, where George Eliot, then Mary Ann Evans, lived from the age of one to 21; her father farmed Griff Farm beside it. The house is now a pub and hotel.

name: Hawkesbury Junction
text: Your train passes near Hawkesbury Junction, on the train's {side}, where the Oxford Canal meets the Coventry Canal, also known as Sutton Stop after a family who kept the lock there in the 19th century. Its engine house of 1821 held a Newcomen steam engine brought from Griff Colliery, where it had already worked for 100 years.

name: Hinckley power station
text: Your train passes the site of a power station, on the train's {side}, that supplied electricity to Hinckley and the wider county from 1913 until the early 1950s. It stood between the railway, whose siding brought its coal, and the Ashby Canal, which brought coal too and gave it cooling water.

name: Claymills Pumping Station
text: Your train passes Claymills Pumping Station, on the train's {side}, a Victorian sewage pumping station designed by James Mansergh. Its four beam engines, built by Gimson and Company of Leicester in 1885, were stopped in 1969 and 1971, and restored to steam one by one between 2000 and 2023.

name: Cropredy
text: Your train passes near Cropredy, on the train's {side}, whose bridge over the River Cherwell gave its name to a Civil War battle in 1644 between King Charles and Sir William Waller's Parliamentarians. Since 1980 the folk rock band Fairport Convention has held a festival on farmland by the village, and one of the church's bells, added in 2007, is named after it.

name: Stourbridge Town station
text: Stourbridge Town station, at one end of this stretch, sits at the end of a branch 0.8 miles long, said to be the shortest branch line in Europe still in use. Its 1879 station was pulled down in 1979 and the line cut back to make room for a bus station; today two Class 139 people movers shuttle to Stourbridge Junction.

name: Wem
text: Your train passes near Wem, on the train's {side}, where the sweet pea was first grown commercially: the nurseryman Henry Eckford set up in the town in 1888, and a sweet pea festival is held there each July. A great fire in 1677 burnt so fiercely that it partly melted the church bells.

name: Hazlitt House
text: Your train passes near Hazlitt House, on the train's {side}, the childhood home of William Hazlitt, one of England's greatest essayists and critics. His father was the town's Unitarian minister, and the house they lived in still stands.

name: Mediolanum
text: Your train passes near the site of Mediolanum, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort and small town on the road between Chester and Wroxeter, where Whitchurch stands today. The town was at its most prosperous in the early 3rd century, and finds from it are shown at the Whitchurch Heritage Centre.

name: The Hive, Worcester
text: Your train passes near The Hive, on the train's {side}, a large golden building that holds Worcester's public library and the University of Worcester's library together, with the county's archives. It cost £60 million and was opened by Queen Elizabeth II on July 11th 2012.

name: Church of St Michael and All Angels, Martin Hussingtree
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Michael and All Angels in Martin Hussingtree, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church largely rebuilt in the early 13th century. The composer Thomas Tomkins, who wrote sacred music in the time of Elizabeth I and James I, was buried in its churchyard on June 9th 1656.

name: Ruskin Pottery
text: Your train passes near the site of the Ruskin Pottery, on the train's {side}, an art pottery founded in 1898 by Edward R. Taylor and run by his son William Howson Taylor. It was famed for its glazes, above all its blood-red sang-de-boeuf and flambé, made by firing copper and iron oxides at high temperature.

name: Soho Foundry
text: Your train passes near Soho Foundry, on the train's {side}, set up beside the Birmingham Canal by Matthew Boulton and James Watt in 1795 to make steam engines. Its planning and standardised parts were so far ahead of their time that the economist Eric Roll wrote that neither Taylor nor Ford devised anything that could not be found at Soho before 1805.

name: Hall of Memory, Birmingham
text: Your train passes near the Hall of Memory, on the train's {side}, in Centenary Square, a Portland stone memorial to the 12,320 people of Birmingham who died in the First World War. Paid for by public donations, it was opened in 1925 to a crowd of 30,000, and stands over a filled-in canal basin.

name: Lifford Reservoir
text: Your train passes near Lifford Reservoir, on the train's {side}, built in 1815 by the Worcester and Birmingham Canal company to make up to Lifford Mill for the water it lost to the canal. It lies where the Stratford-upon-Avon Canal meets the Worcester and Birmingham, and holds tench, carp, pike and eels.

name: Hazelwell
text: Your train passes Hazelwell, on the train's {side}, named after the Hazel Well, a spring beside the River Rea, and home of the Hazelwell family from at least 1325. Its corn mill on the Rea, first recorded in 1704, made gun barrels from 1783 until 1886.

name: Shrewley
text: Your train passes near Shrewley, on the train's {side}, a village with no church whose parish holds Hatton station and the triangle of lines just west of it, used by trains to and from Stratford-upon-Avon. Its pub, the Durham Ox, was once known for its Marrow Sunday harvest celebration.

name: The Ridding
text: Your train passes near The Ridding, on the train's {side}, a Victorian country house in Bentham built in 1857 to 1860 for Baldwin Harry Bent. It is in the Scottish Baronial style, the only building in that style designed by the Lancaster architect E. G. Paley.

name: St Margaret's Church, High Bentham
text: Your train passes St Margaret's Church, on the train's {side}, built in High Bentham in 1837 and enlarged in 1901 and 1902 by the Lancaster architects Austin and Paley. It closed in 2012 and has been turned into two homes.

name: Eldroth
text: Your train passes near Eldroth, on the train's {side}, a village of only 12 buildings in its main part, counted a village rather than a hamlet because it has a church. It lies just inside the Forest of Bowland Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and its stone village hall opened in 2000.

name: St Mary's Church, Long Preston
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, the parish church of Long Preston, probably built in the late 14th century and listed Grade I. Inside are a late 17th-century pulpit, a Romanesque font with a canopy of 1726 and stained glass by Jean-Baptiste Capronnier.

name: The Folly, Settle
text: Your train passes near The Folly, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed 17th-century house on the main street. Restored by a local trust and opened to the public in 2001, it holds the Museum of North Craven Life, with displays on the Settle to Carlisle Railway.

name: Langcliffe Hoffmann kiln
text: Your train passes near the Hoffmann kiln at Langcliffe, on the train's {side}, built in 1873 for the Craven Lime Company once the Settle to Carlisle line had made heavy industry possible. Its 22 chambers burnt limestone continuously in a circuit that took about six weeks; it closed for good in 1939.

name: Ribblehead Quarry
text: Your train passes near Ribblehead Quarry, on the train's {side}, whose limestone was first used to build this railway. In the early 20th century its stone went to North East England for iron and steel making, and even into toothpaste and household cleaners; it reopened in 1943 to produce limestone for farms.
